per_case.playbook: 1) Isolate 192.168.100.147 from the network (EDR/quarantine or switch-port ACL) to stop the automated loop. 2) Capture a full packet trace of the .147 traffic and preserve it for analysis. 3) Identify the process/agent on .147 generating the requests and scan for botnet/IoT malware (flow UIDs carry a BOTIOT label). 4) Review web server logs on 192.168.100.3 and 192.168.100.7 for exploitation, credential stuffing, or successful compromise attributable to .147. 5) If .3/.7 show signs of compromise, escalate to a separate incident for those hosts. 6) Reimage or factory-reset the device before returning it to the network, and rate-limit/segment IoT assets from internal web servers.

Isolate 192.168.100.148 from the network (EDR/switch port containment) while preserving volatile memory and a forensic image. Pull the web/auth logs on 192.168.100.3 to enumerate the 999 requests, identify response codes (look for any 200/302 among the 710-byte rejections indicating a successful attempt), and determine which account or endpoint parameters were sprayed. Force password reset for any account targeted, scan 192.168.100.148 for malware or unauthorized automation scripts that generated the traffic, review for additional internal lateral targets, and require re-imaging or verified remediation before reconnecting the host.

Isolate host 192.168.100.149 from the network (EDR/switch port isolation) while preserving a memory and disk image for forensics; hunt for the implant and persistence that receives traffic on TCP 4444 and 49160 and identify/block the C2 peer 192.168.100.6; capture and analyze the payload volume delivered to the host; review web server logs on 192.168.100.3 and 192.168.100.7 for the sprayed HTTP requests and check those servers for compromise; block egress/ingress to port 4444 and reset credentials used from this host.

1) Isolate 192.168.100.150 from the network (quarantine VLAN / EDR containment) while preserving volatile evidence. 2) Capture a memory image and the web access logs from 192.168.100.3:80 to recover the full request corpus and confirm whether any request returned a 2xx/5xx anomaly indicating successful brute force or exploitation. 3) Triage 192.168.100.150 for implant/fuzzing tooling, scheduled tasks, and anomalous processes; identify the parent process generating the 992 requests. 4) Hunt for the same request corpus or byte-pattern across all other internal hosts to find additional compromised siblings. 5) Verify the single NTP flow to 27.124.125.251 is legitimate corporate time sync and not covert C2. 6) Reset any credentials stored on the isolated host and audit authentication logs for lateral movement. 7) Re-enable threat-intel API access to enrich future verdicts.

1) Confirm with the asset owner that 192.168.100.3 is the IoT/telemetry broker-gateway for .148/.149/.150 and that 13.54.166.67:8883 is the sanctioned AWS IoT Core endpoint. 2) If confirmed, tune/suppress FLOW-005 'Beacon receiver' for this collector and add the AWS IoT broker to the allow-list baseline. 3) Baseline the uniform ~4.28s / 5-11-packet polling pattern as normal so future deviations (payload growth, duration drift, new ports) trigger instead. 4) No isolation or blocking; re-open only if endpoint or firewall telemetry later shows compromise on .3, or if new external destinations or non-8883 outbound flows appear.

1) Network-isolate 192.168.100.6 (EDR/switch port containment) while preserving forensic image and memory capture. 2) Block east-west traffic to TCP 4444 and the 49160 channel; collect full packet capture for the .6<->.149 sessions. 3) Triage hosts 192.168.100.147, .148, .149, .150 for the same implant/scanning behavior and isolate any confirmed infected node. 4) Review 192.168.100.3 web-server logs for the 47MB upload activity and check for webshell/upload abuse. 5) Hunt for the initial access vector, reset credentials used by .6, and re-image after forensic capture. 6) Tune FLOW-005 to direction-aware logic so it reports the scanning source as well as the receiving endpoint.

1) Block 162.208.22.34 inbound/outbound at the perimeter firewall and add DNS/SNI/proxy deny-all for the peer. 2) Hunt retrospective C2 traffic for all 6 internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .12, .14, .15) across full NetFlow history for fixed-byte-profile sessions to any external /22, not just this IP. 3) Escalate to host IR on 192.168.10.5 first (highest flow volume, single-peer-only traffic): memory/disk forensic acquisition, autorun & scheduled-task review, and hash the recurring payload sizes (358/1150 fwd bytes, 3776/4356 bwd bytes) for beacon-jitter fingerprinting. 4) Pull EDR agent coverage on the six hosts since endpoint_events is empty for this window — telemetry gap is itself a finding. 5) Monitor for destination rotation/DGA failover and re-blocking after block deployment.

Close the alert as a false positive (NetBIOS broadcast traffic to subnet broadcast address). Suppress/tune FLOW-005 to exclude dest_port 137/138 UDP to x.x.x.255 broadcast addresses, and optionally recommend disabling or scoping NetBIOS broadcast (NBNS/NetBIOS-DGM) on workstations in the 192.168.10.0/24 segment to reduce noise. No host isolation or IP blocking required.

Suppress/tune FLOW-002, FLOW-003 and FLOW-005 thresholds for internal DNS/NTP service hosts (whitelist 192.168.10.3 <-> 192.168.10.1 UDP/53 and UDP/123), document the false positive, and optionally enable DNS query logging on 192.168.10.3 for periodic anomaly review; no containment action required.

1) Close the alert as a false positive with the above evidence attached. 2) Tune the FLOW-002 sensor rule to baseline per-host DNS query rates (or suppress when dest is an internal resolver on udp/53 with successful responses) since ~0.7 qps triggered a 2643-flow count. 3) Fix the alert normalization bug that reports protocol 'tcp' and 'Attempted Administrator Privilege Gain' for UDP DNS flows. 4) No action on host 192.168.10.5 or resolver 192.168.10.3; optionally confirm 192.168.10.3 is the sanctioned internal DNS server and review the 24 flows to 104.254.87.60:443 (zero-byte payloads, short duration, 1913-2321s) as a low-priority follow-up if that peer is unrecognized.

Isolate 192.168.10.8 from the network immediately (quarantine via EDR/NAC, preserve host for forensics). Capture volatile data and memory image, then hunt for the scanning tooling and any dropped payloads. Review full packet capture for the 205.174.165.73:444 sessions to determine what data left the environment (12.66 MB egress) and block that peer at the perimeter. Audit 192.168.10.9, 192.168.10.12, and 192.168.10.16 for exposed/open ports, successful connections, and signs of follow-on compromise, and check the internal DNS resolver 192.168.10.3 logs for abusive or tunneled query patterns from this host. Reset any credentials used from the host, and escalate to Tier 3 for lateral-movement scope assessment.

Close as benign for 192.168.10.9: verify 192.168.10.9 DNS resolver settings and confirm 192.168.10.3 is the authorized internal DNS/NTP server; suppress/tune FLOW-002 internal DNS volume threshold and FLOW-005 receiver-direction signature (count inbound scan attempts as target-victim, not C2). Open a separate investigation on 192.168.10.8 as the scanning source (656-port sweep) and correlate its outbound traffic for follow-on C2; monitor 192.168.10.9 for signs of post-scan exploitation, and if that host shows malicious local activity, escalate to ISOLATE_HOST.

1) Block 23.60.139.27 at the perimeter firewall/proxy (TCP/80) immediately and deny all egress to it. 2) Identify and rescue-detect beaconing artifacts on all 11 internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .12, .14, .15, .16, .17, .19, .25, .51) — review running processes, scheduled tasks, and autoruns for the HTTP client generating ~5.4s and ~110s interval requests to that IP. 3) Pull full-period DNS logs to confirm whether the IP is reached directly or via a domain, and hunt sibling IPs/domains from the same infrastructure. 4) Capture a PCAP of one beaconing host to fingerprint the User-Agent and URI pattern for IOC creation. 5) Isolate any host where the beaconing process is positively identified as malware. 6) Escalate to Tier 3 / IR if a C2 implant is confirmed on any endpoint.

1) Block 50.63.243.230 at the egress firewall/proxy for all internal segments (deny TCP/80 and any other ports). 2) Sinkhole/alert on any residual DNS or IP-based connections to it. 3) Scope the beaconing population: pull full flow history for the 10-11 internal source hosts and check for payload variations or secondary C2 peers. 4) Acquire memory/process and autorun telemetry from each beaconing host to identify the implant, then isolate hosts showing confirmed implant behavior (ISOLATE_HOST playbook). 5) Re-run IP reputation/CTI enrichment on 50.63.243.230 once threat-intel access is restored, and review proxy logs for the initial compromise vector.
